title: Cats in the dark: A review of our current knowledge of the deep‐sea catshark genus Apristurus
content:
Abstract

The deep-sea catsharks in the genus Apristurus (Pentanchidae) constitute one of the most species-rich yet least resolved elasmobranch lineages. Herein, we utilised a systematic literature search to synthesise current knowledge on their diversity, morphology, phylogeny, distribution, ecology, reproduction and threats, and outline priorities for research aligned with the UN Decade of Ocean Science. The genus currently comprises 43 described extant species and three extinct taxa. Morphologically, Apristurus species share cephalic dorso-ventral compression, broad spatulate snouts and diagnostic labial-furrow states; meristics (including vertebral counts) and egg-capsule morphology provide additional taxonomic signal. Morphological ratios and fin shapes are also valuable for identification. Phylogenetic evidence generally supports monophyly of the genus and recovery of three species groups (brunneus, spongiceps, longicephalus), although some recent morphology-led hypotheses warrant further genomic testing. Apristurus is circumglobal (excluding polar seas and the Mediterranean), occupies depths ca. 24–2652 m and functions primarily as a generalist mesopredator, with region- and species-specific trophic specialisation. Reproductive ecology is oviparous; egg capsules commonly aggregate on structurally complex substrates (e.g., sponges and corals) where local hydrodynamics likely enhance embryonic ventilation. Fossil egg cases at cold seeps indicate long-standing associations with complex deep-sea habitats. Major threats to the genus arise from deep-sea trawl bycatch and emerging seabed industries. Threats are exacerbated by genus life-history traits (prolonged development, low fecundity) which imply high sensitivity, though many species remain listed as Least Concern owing to a paucity of data due to the depths at which the genus lives. Key research gaps identified include the need for a robust, integrative taxonomy; publicly accessible genetic reference libraries; in situ behavioural and life-history observations; quantification of bycatch and post-release mortality; and assessment of climate and mining impacts on nursery habitats. We provide a consolidated baseline of information to assist with accelerated discovery, identification and conservation of Apristurus across its global range.
